lesson.title: A Pairs with T, G Pairs with C: The Rules That Make Replication Possible
lesson.summary: Base pairing rules describe which nitrogenous bases bond to which across the two strands of DNA, adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine, a specific and predictable chemistry that makes each strand a template for reconstructing its exact partner.
lesson.body:
The double helix chapter established that the two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases pointing inward from each backbone. Base pairing rules specify exactly which bases can bond to which. Adenine pairs specifically with thymine, connected by two hydrogen bonds, and guanine pairs specifically with cytosine, connected by three hydrogen bonds. This pairing is not interchangeable. Adenine does not pair with guanine or cytosine, and thymine does not pair with cytosine or guanine, because the shapes and hydrogen bonding groups of the bases only line up correctly in the adenine-thymine and guanine-cytosine combinations.

Part of the reason for this specific pairing pattern is chemical geometry. Adenine and guanine are purines, larger bases built from two fused carbon-nitrogen rings, while thymine and cytosine are pyrimidines, smaller bases built from a single ring. Pairing a purine with a pyrimidine in each case, rather than purine with purine or pyrimidine with pyrimidine, keeps the width of the helix perfectly consistent all the way along its length, since a purine-pyrimidine pair always spans roughly the same distance between the two backbones. A purine-purine pair would be too wide and a pyrimidine-pyrimidine pair would be too narrow to fit the uniform, evenly spaced backbone geometry described in the previous chapter.

This is also the molecular explanation behind Chargaff's rules mentioned earlier: because every adenine on one strand is matched with a thymine on the other, the total amount of adenine in a DNA molecule always equals the total amount of thymine, and because every guanine is matched with a cytosine, the total amount of guanine always equals the total amount of cytosine. This does not mean adenine plus thymine together equal guanine plus cytosine together. The overall proportion of A-T pairs versus G-C pairs varies between species and even between regions of a genome, and because G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds compared to the two in an A-T pair, DNA regions richer in G-C content tend to require more energy to separate the two strands.

Base pairing rules make it possible to determine the sequence of an entire complementary strand just from one strand, remembering that the two strands are antiparallel, as covered in the double helix chapter. Take the strand 5'-ATGCCTAG-3'. Reading it in order, A pairs with T, T pairs with A, G pairs with C, C pairs with G, C pairs with G, T pairs with A, A pairs with T, and G pairs with C. Writing these paired bases directly underneath, in the same left to right order, gives 3'-TACGGATC-5', which is the complementary strand running in the opposite chemical direction, exactly as required for the strands to be antiparallel. Written the conventional way, starting from its own 5' end, that same complementary strand reads 5'-CTAGGCAT-3'. This complementary, antiparallel pairing is what allows each strand of a DNA molecule to serve as an exact template for reconstructing its partner, which is the foundation for how DNA is replicated with such high fidelity every time a cell divides.
